doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

chapter: Kai and J.J., Bohemia and Embers
title: Missing Cannonball's night, then subbing at the Embers with Tyree Glenn and Jo Jones
summary: Substituting for Hank Jones at the Embers, Erroll Garner's dynamics, Jo Jones defending him against Tyree Glenn's showmanship, then Gigi Gryce's group.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: And we went in the studio and Percy Heath played on it. Okay so fast forward again and here I am with Oscar Pettiford and all these, and I was not there the night, bad luck, that Cannonball came in.
I was just going to ask.
I wasn’t there that night. Damn.
Who was taking your place do you know?

I don’t know probably Horace Silver or somebody. I don’t know. He broke the piano. I remember one night Horace broke the piano. It was a little spinet and — oh he was playing opposite me, that’s right — and all the hammers had been knocked off — it was a mess. I loved Horace, I thought he was great. And then I used to work in the Embers. One night I got a — Hank Jones, one of my all time heroes, he’s incredible, he was so in demand that he would take, say yes to three jobs and then at the last minute he’d decide which one he was going to take, then he’d make these panicky calls to get — so one night he called — would I sub for him at The Embers. The Embers was a fancy steakhouse on the East side where they had soft jazz, muted trumpet, Jonah Jones and so on and so on. But they had Art Tatum in there once playing for the diners. They didn’t even keep quiet for him. One pianist that shut that room up — it was Erroll Garner. Because he did it with dynamics. He’d be roaring away and all of a sudden he’d drop down.

That’s right. He was a magician. Not that Tatum — so Hank says, “Can you go on and take this” so it turned out to be like two months or something. It was Tyree Glenn, Papa Jo Jones who was the real leader, Tyree was the front man, and Tommy Potter. And it was very well structured and Jo didn’t care too much for Tyree I think because Tyree used to really lay it on thick.

He’d roll his eyes around and Texas fat cats would come in and they’d say to me, “Whatchu doin up there boy?” But Jo Jones would come to my defense, he’d say, “He’s playing the piano, that’s what he’s doing. Go away.” But Tyree was like, take any requests—
You mean like he was doing the Vaudeville thing almost.

Yes. He was a terrific musician but he was doing that. But it was a good job. Then I worked there with Charlie Shavers and then I would up playing with that rhythm section down back at the Bohemia with Lucky Thompson and I was in Gigi’s Jazz Lab group. There is a guy writing a book about him, upstate somewhere.
On Gigi. He interviewed me, yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
